source.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
source.authors: Abir Harrasse; Florent Draye; Punya Syon Pandey; Zhijing Jin; Bernhard Scholkopf

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper and supplementary material; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Applies cross-layer feature dictionaries and attribution analysis to multilingual LLMs, reporting results about features recovered in those models. It extends feature-based interpretability to a new setting, rather than testing toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test superposition geometry, feature sparsity versus capacity, or one-dimensional versus multidimensional features. Its relevant results concern CLT-recovered features in multilingual LLMs. Results cited from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study uses cross-layer transcoders (sparse feature dictionaries) as a tool to study multilingual processing. Its results concern the language organization of CLT features: entropy across layers, feature overlap and language-feature interventions. It does not test whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features or superposition. The replacement score (0.75–0.8) and explained variance (>70%) are quality checks and training stop criteria for the tool, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that middle layers form a shared multilingual space and that a small set of high-frequency late-layer features decodes language identity. They say this structure also appears without English. Interventions on these features shift output language. They attribute non-English gaps to tokenization and weaker downstream activations, which finetuning strengthens.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-layer transcoders, attribution graphs, and multilingual LLMs trained or analyzed across languages; it does not use toy networks, sparse-feature competition, or the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported entropy organization varies with model depth: the 4-layer TinyStories model lacks the rise-and-fall pattern. Feature overlap changes with English training proportion. The Llama final-layer entropy result is noted as potentially affected by CLT training dynamics.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper notes that its primary analysis uses relatively small models (68M and 177M parameters), with only LLaMA-3.2-1B as a larger-model validation; production-scale generality is uncertain. CLT training is computationally costly, and sensitivity to seeds and implementation details is not exhaustively characterized. The relevant dictionary is a CLT rather than an SAE, and several results are qualitative or given only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Results on language-task circuit examples, tokenization, model-diffing, and language performance were not included where they did not measure dictionary feature recovery or the feature behavior specified by V4.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity-competition analysis of polysemantic neurons.
All: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
The study does not test whether features are spread across neurons or whether dictionary features are genuinely recovered. CLT reconstruction is reported only as a tool-quality check.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity; the seed sensitivity of the CLTs is not characterized.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label should be dropped: using a CLT successfully as an analysis tool is T4 use, not a test. Appendix J.2 speculates that Chinese 'consumes a larger portion of the model's capacity'. This is an untested interpretive remark, not evidence for V2.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse features exceeding dimensions, overlap geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Whether polysemantic neurons result from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study uses CLTs, not SAEs; it does not measure feature spread across neurons, compare dictionary methods, or establish generality across production-scale LLMs.
It does not establish whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units. Its model-diff analysis concerns CLT features, not SAE feature validity.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: GPT-2, TinyStories, and Llama-3.2-1B CLTs (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: GPT-2 and TinyStories trained from scratch; Llama-3.2-1B pretrained
rows.operation_detail: Measured CLT replacement scores as a reconstruction-performance check.
rows.note: The paper reports this result for its CLTs collectively; it does not give a separate score for each model in the supplied text. CLTs are feature dictionaries, but are not SAEs.
rows.check: This is a CLT quality check and stopping criterion, not a result on V4. Training stopped once explained variance passed 70%, so the value is partly a selection value.

rows.subject: Multilingual GPT-2 models
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation-rate-weighted multilingual entropy of CLT features across layers.
rows.measure: Average weighted multilingual feature entropy across layers
rows.value: Low in early layers, rises sharply in middle layers, then decreases toward output layers; described as robust across data mixtures.
rows.note: The reported trend is a summary across mixtures; no separate numerical values for each mixture are stated in the text.
rows.check: This measures the language entropy of CLT features across layers (multilinguality), not superposition or feature recovery.

rows.subject: Multilingual TinyStories model
rows.operation_detail: Measured multilingual entropy of CLT features across layers.
rows.value: The rise-and-fall pattern is absent; all layers have similar entropy scores.
rows.note: This reports a different entropy pattern, not a failure to recover features with a dictionary.
rows.check: This is a multilingual-entropy pattern, not a superposition measure.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Measured multilingual entropy of CLT features across layers.
rows.value: The paper reports the same general pattern in the Llama-3.2-1B CLT; it notes a final-layer jump that may be due to training dynamics.
rows.note: The paper cautions that some final-layer features have small activations but affect the multilingual score.
rows.check: This is a multilingual-entropy pattern in Llama; it is unrelated to the claim's versions.

rows.subject: GPT-2 trained on non-English data
rows.operation_detail: Measured weighted multilingual entropy of CLT features across layers.

conditions.value: 25% French, 25% German, 25% Arabic, 25% Chinese; no English

rows.baseline: English-dominant models, including 20% English plus other languages
rows.value: The paper reports an identical characteristic rise-and-fall pattern, with peak entropy in layers 5–6.
rows.note: This is evidence about cross-language organization of CLT features, not about superposition geometry.
rows.check: This concerns the language organization of features in a model trained without English, not superposition.

rows.subject: Multilingual GPT-2 models
rows.operation_detail: Compared overlap of language-specific CLT features with English-specific features.

conditions.value: French, German, Chinese, and Arabic; reported across non-English languages

rows.measure: Percentage overlap of non-English language-specific features with English-specific features
rows.value: Approximately 77% at 20% English and 84% at 90% English
rows.note: The paper describes these values as applying across the non-English languages; separate language-specific values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: This is the overlap of language-specific features between languages; it does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Multilingual GPT-2 models
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise overlap among language-specific CLT features for non-English language pairs.
rows.measure: Pairwise overlap among non-English language-specific features
rows.value: Average overlap was 89% at 20% English; at 90% English the gap from overlap with English was described as near parity.
rows.note: The paper reports an average at 20% and a qualitative comparison at 90%; it does not state a separate numerical value for every pair in the text.
rows.check: This is pairwise language-feature overlap; it does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Multilingual LLMs analyzed in the attribution graphs
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed late-layer language features for one language and added target-language feature activations from translated prompts.

conditions.value: source-language feature zeroing plus target-language feature addition

rows.value: The paper says target-language logit rank substantially increases; perfect prediction typically requires additional feature modifications or sweeping intervention values.
rows.note: The text does not give a model-by-model result or numerical logit-rank values.
rows.check: This is a steering intervention on output language with no superposition measure. The subject is unspecified and no numbers are given.

rows.subject: Multilingual GPT-2 and LLaMA models
rows.stage_stated: GPT-2 trained from scratch; LLaMA-3.2-1B pretrained
rows.operation_detail: Measured token activation frequency for language-specific CLT features.
rows.measure: Fraction of tokens activated by language features within their respective languages
rows.value: A small number of features activate on 50–100% of tokens within each language; the paper also says most high-frequency CLT features are language-specific.
rows.note: The paper does not give separate values by model or feature in the text.
rows.check: This is the activation frequency of language features; it is unrelated to the versions.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CLT analyses of the multilingual GPT-2 models, non-English GPT-2 model, and Llama-3.2-1B
reader_labels.reason: The paper trains sparse CLT feature dictionaries, reports reconstruction scores and analyzes recovered features across layers and languages; interventions on selected features also alter target-language logit rank (r1, r2, r4, r5, r6, r7, r8, r9). This supports dictionary-recoverable features in the tested models, not SAE-specific claims or superposition.
